items.body: Thematically, Post Dub Cities hearkens back to Future Sound of London’s Dead Cities, while tonally it recalls Murcof’s Rememberanza. Adriano Zanni‘s vision of a future world is the cold reflection of a present reality in which many places are already deserted: peeling houses, dilapidated storefronts, bombed villages. At one time, they teemed with life. Once humans have no more use for a city, they abandon it, leaving only rubble and questionable specters. The reasons may be as far afield as the loss of jobs, the evaporation of resources, or a campaign of bombs. More than anything, Post Dub Cities is an album of mood. Zanni wants his listeners to be uncomfortable, to regard these cities as one does the stone wreckage of Ozymandius. From the opening notes of “Crisopoli” (also the first single), he casts a spell of resignation and despair. The pace is slow, but not sluggish; the beats restrained, but not soft. Someone has to bear witness. In “Pyramiden,” the tone grows harsher, with amplified whispers, clacking pipes and cavernous echoes. Were it not for the dub timbres, one might call this industrial or post-industrial music. Each piece seems to hide another piece behind it: a subdued rhythm, a moving shadow. In “Centralia,” sharp beats stumble like scavengers sifting through wreckage. These visitors may not be human, or even humanoid; in Alan Weisman’s classic The World Without Us, everything from roaches to raccoons reclaims its own. Rust abrades metal; girders bend; branches break through glass. The accompanying pdf is essential to the release. Referencing Calvino and Marcelli, Zanni writes of the empty city as an “echo chamber,” an image reflected in the music. A hundred pages of sublime black and white photographs follow, captured in cities around the world over the past two decades. The unifying feature is the lack of any human presence, as if scrubbed from existence (insert sci-fi theory here). Proof of humanity’s presence remains, but without context. In Zanni’s own words: “memory without recollection, structure without use, body without inhabitants.” In response, the music is architectural: one imagines a grid in which beats and notes are purposely placed. Belgrade, Vienna, Amsterdam, Barcelona, Berlin, Dublin, Sarajevo, Rome, London, Prague, Madrid, Krakow, Istanbul, Lisbon, Palermo and more, all deserted: buildings empty, rollercoasters stilled, markets abandoned, art left to dissolve. Not a single vehicle is visible, even on the highway. One can see what humans have done, but not where they have gone. In what seems to be the final image, a massive wall of chairs is ready for a group of patrons who never arrive. Capturing these images must have required remarkable patience and timing. The last bonus track, “San Zhi Pod City,” offers a surprise: the appearance of a human voice. Even this turns out to be a loop, a remnant, an echo. But Zanni does have a final trick up his sleeve: on page 99, the people reappear, filling the square. The last four images show humanity wall to literal wall: perhaps too much humanity, suggesting a reason for its removal or demise. As much as one pores through “Kadykchan” and “San Zhi Pod City” for a matching restoration, one cannot hear it in the grooves. The listener is left to ponder whether the detritus of humanity might hold any intrinsic value, or if it is only sound and fury, signifying nothing. (Richard Allen)

items.body: Tiiva This Could Be A Start UK producer's soundtrack to an imaginary video game delivers a maximalist hyper pop sucker punch blue fifty-nine/this could be a start by Tiiva Video game design and hyperpop share a clear sonic DNA, defined by maximalism, shape-shifting identities and non-linear structures. From the music genre’s inception, its most formative artists have embedded game tropes into their digital soundscapes. With This Could Be A Start, Lake District-based producer and game designer Tiiva delivers a compelling addition to this well-trodden collision of spaces. The result is a euphoric, emotionally resonant record, despite occasional forays into over-reverence toward the pop pioneers it draws from. items.body: In August of this year, New Focus Recordings released New Music for Two Voices, an impressive collection of acapella vocal music by sopranos Susan Narucki and Kirsten Ashley Wiest. This lavish album features a full hour masterful singing of six contemporary works, including three world premiere recordings. Susan Narucki is an accomplished soprano who has appeared as a soloist with the Cleveland Orchestra, Los Angeles Philharmonic, the San Francisco Symphony, among many other international appearances. She is presently on the faculty of the Department of Music at UC San Diego. Kirsten Ashley Wiest is an award-winning coloratura soprano who has performed and recorded alongside numerous GRAMMY winners, the Los Angeles Philharmonic, San Diego Symphony, Bang on a Can All-Stars and the Partch ensemble, among many others. Kirsten currently teaches voice at San Bernardino Valley College and University of California Riverside, New Music for Two Voices is a deep dive into the cutting edge of virtuoso vocal technique as it intersects with contemporary musical composition. The album is accompanied by excellent liner notes, full translations of the texts and biographical notes on the composers and the performers. The outstanding sound engineering is by Andrew Munsey and Kristina Tran. The first track on the album is come sempre (2025), by Dutch composer Rozalie Hirs. Although written just last year, the liner notes inform that this piece “…evokes music of an earlier time, with shifting tonal centers and interwoven melodic lines..” Running at over 7 minutes, it is one of the longer works of the entire album and is a world premiere. come sempre features two voices singing separately in Italian, sometimes together and sometimes in a call and response pattern. The vocal lines are often independent and weave in and around each other seamlessly in a series of lovely harmonies. There is no accompaniment anywhere in this album so the two singers must rely on their internal sense of rhythm and pitch. Where crisp phrases are present, these are always clean and punchy. Nothing ragged or blurry here; the notes are precise and balanced. As the piece proceeds it gradually increases in complexity, summoning ever greater technique. The singing by these two confident voices, however, is always controlled throughout. The poems of El trino persistente by Javier Tafur González are the inspiration for TRINOS, a series of twelve miniature works by Colombian composer Alba Potes. Commissioned by Susan Narucki in 2024, all are less than one minute long, yet these pieces sparkle like brilliant gems. The liner notes state that “Each of the twelve settings seems to capture a moment in time—by turns, lyrical, nostalgic, jubilant, hopeful.” “TRINOS: I. Jazmin” is the first of the twelve pieces and although less than a minute in length, it sets the standard for the precision and vocal technique that is heard throughout the entire work. A high vocal tone opens, then falls rapidly in pitch as a second voice joins in a middle register with dissonance. The singers must rely on their own intuition for pitch and timing – there are no accompanying chords or common rhythms. The overall feeling is one of welcome and portent. Although less than a minute in length, this first piece sets a high bar for vocal artistry. Other pieces in the work are similarly concise and illustrate the consistent level of virtuosity brought to bear by Wiest and Narucki. “TRINOS: II. Entra illuminando la casa”, at just 32 seconds in length ,is intense, with many jumps and leaps in the two voices. It shines like a fiery jewel. “TRINOS: IV. No saldré” features a middle register voice together with a lower voice in close harmony. Stretches of unusual dissonances challenge the singers, but are navigated successfully. “TRINOS: VI. Timida flor” opens with a strong voice soaring up very high with impressive power and good control. “TRINOS: VII. Ven, anclemos” is soft, with almost mournful feeling and quietly sentimental. The text, even in English translation, is perfect: “Come, let us anchor now hands entwined.” “TRINOS: IX. Se hundió el buque” by contrast, is completely different. A quiet, solo voice is heard in a middle register, reserved and subdued. The lyrics are more spoken than sung, producing a purposeful and deliberate sensibility. “TRINOS: XI. Podemos estar juntos” is another solo piece with a strong voice crying out as if in sadness. The singing here is expressive, yet delivered with great clarity. The final piece in the work is “TRINOS: XII. En los hilos”, a duet with the lower voice in sustained tones underneath a soaring, coloratura voice. The dissonances in the harmonies add a powerful, melancholy feeling to this. TRINOS is a masterful collection of small pieces that each deliver an emotional punch from the virtuosity of the performers. The third work on the album is From the Grammar of Dreams (1988), by Kaija Saariaho and consists of five pieces based on two separate texts from the American poet Sylvia Plath. The liner notes tell us that “The five duets demonstrate Saariaho’s unique compositional language, with its attention to fine gradations of vocal color, intricacy and flexibility of gesture, and a nearly overwhelming range of emotional expression.” The first duet, labeled simply “I”, opens with strange and painful sounds in the lower voice with struggling vocals in the second voice as if forcing out the words and notes. Leaps and jumps are heard in the upper voice accompanied by sustained and plaintive sounds from the lower. Just a little over 2 minutes long, this piece is expressively weird and haunting.“II”, the second piece in From the Grammar of Dreams begins with two sets of spoken words heard simultaneously. This is somewhat chaotic as there is no common tones or phrasing. One voice includes some rather gruesome details, as if recounting a nightmare. The voices are alternately speaking and singing and often very agitated. The music is complex and dynamic, yet confidently delivered. The third duet, “III” is soft and melodic; completely different in character from the previous pieces. There is lovely harmony in the two voices with lots of sustained notes and dramatic gestures. There is a welcome and mysterious feeling to this. “IV” opens with scratchy, breathy sounds followed by strong vocal music. The voices jump and soar as each part bounces breathlessly off the other. The two voices devolve in a sort of shouting match just before the piece concludes with a few short breaths. Amazing technique here. The final duet, “V”, begins with a series of sustained notes in both voices sung in a high register with prominent vibrato. The sounds loop around each other independently in pitch and dynamic. This produces an eerie feeling at times but is mostly strongly declarative. The fourth work on the album is NauðaR Níu [The Nine Needs] (2025), by Jeffrey Holmes. This collection of nine pieces is based on old Norse Runic carvings (ca. 5th through 12th century), as compiled and translated by the composer. As with the other works in this album, each piece is short, ranging from 37 seconds to a little over three and a half minutes. As explained in the liner notes, NauðaR Níu features some unusual accompaniment: “Throughout, the vocalists play a variety of percussion instruments; the sound of metal, skin, wood and natural materials contributing to the sense of a vast primeval landscape.” The opening piece of NauðaR Níu, titled simply “I”, starts with soft tones by two voices. As this one minute piece proceeds, a gentle gong sound and some light percussion are heard; a subtle and mysterious beginning. “II” sets a completely different tone. A sharp drum rap begins, serving as a starting exclamation point. The two voices weave in and around each other in sustained tones amid much howling and spooky vocals. Another series of bangs from the drum and a woodblock add to the unnerving atmosphere. “III” returns to a more settled and soothing feeling. A low sustained vocal in one voice is made more expressive by the light tinkling of chimes. Very mystical and solemn with lovely vocals and reverential sentiment. “IV” continues in a sacred feeling, opening with an Ahhh sound in a single voice. Another voice joins in, accompanied by quiet gong tones and a low drone. The exotic – almost Asian – feel of this is supported by devout vocals, gentle chimes and percussion. “V” continues in the exotic groove and returns to the more forward style with drum raps and sharp woodblock beats. The voices seeming to chant with out words but in eerie, sustained tones. There is a decidedly spectral and anxious feeling to this. “VI” returns to the more subdued refinement heard in “IV”, with a soft opening and chimes. A sudden drum strike with wood block recalls the mood in “II”. A gong is heard between the sustained and almost mournful vocals. There is a sacred, worshipful feel to this. “VII” continues with chimes and a high, plaintive opening vocal. The top voice soars in very high, airy sweeps. More chimes accompany. The excellent singing, heard in very high registers, is controlled, on pitch and does not lose its power. “VIII” opens with a strong drum strike and woodblock rap. Loud, almost screaming vocals are heard, as if in great surprise. A palpable sense of danger and fear is present. Loud drum and woodblock strikes accompanied by long, descending sweeps of vocals paint a convincing musical portrait of fear and despair, This sets the stage for the final section, “IX” which opens with a haunting vocal solo , soon joined by the second voice in call and response. The voices are subdued with somber descending pitches and accompanied by drum strikes, chimes and gong strikes. All elements of the various sections seemingly combine into a sense of acceptance and fateful resignation. Beautiful, expressive singing is heard as the vocals fade to the finish. With NauðaR Níu, Jeffrey Holmes has forged a vibrant musical connection between the Old Norse culture and our own.The next work on the album is a collection of five short pieces titled Two Walking (1994) by French composer Pascal Dusapin. The text for Two Walking is by American writer Gertrude Stein and the work was originally conceived by Dusapin as a study for his chamber opera To Be Sung. The opening piece of Dusapin’s collection, titled “I. How many little wings” begins with a single lyrical voice followed closely be a second vocal, almost as an echo. Now the higher voice soars in a sustained upward arc with text following in both voices. The vocals bounce and dance around each other, evoking birdlike acrobatics on the wing. As the tempo increases the text becomes louder and more frenetic. A sudden slowing towards the finish provides the listener with a soft landing. “ II. Kiss my lips” begins with a quiet clicking and two voices in a sort of conversation. There is a whispering and intimate feel to this, sung as if in secret. “III. May, June” opens with a long solo note followed by the second voice entering slightly below in a counter melody. Now the notes in each voice volley back and forth effectively. As the text moves faster, crisply sung in short, quick phrases, the result is a pleasingly complex texture that does not sacrifice the beautiful harmonies. “IV. A scene in singing” has both voices starting together but soon singing separate lines. Short snappy phrases are heard in places and at times the harmony is unusual, but the overall effect is both lovely and abstract. The final piece in the Dusapin work is “ V. It seems to be”. Two voices in lower register open in syncopated rhythms and the separate vocal lines produce an engaging, crunchy texture. The pitches and harmony are controlled and balanced, even with the lively phrasing. “ V. It seems to be” is a fine finish to an intriguing work. The concluding work on the album is Melisande (2022), by Marti Epstein, the longest piece at almost 13 minutes. Inspired by the Debussy opera, Epstein re-imagines the story as if told through Melisande’s own experience, rather than as a reflection of others. In this interpretation, “the two sopranos alternate between extending and finishing each other’s words, functioning as a single unit, or singing passages with overlapping, contrapuntal lines that give way to moments of ecstatic release.” Melisande opens with two sustained voices in a delicate harmony and dynamics that vary intriguingly. The vocals become more active, with independent lines weaving in and around each other in a call and response pattern. By 4:10 the voices are singing in common phrases in an effective contrast to the opening. The upper voice is especially impressive, exhibiting a fine tone with strength and confidence. By 7:10 the vocals are in solid harmony and declarative text sung expressively in middle registers. The lines diverge and become occasionally independent, one often following the other. The duet singing here is especially disciplined and precise. At a slowing of the tempo, Melisande fades quietly to its finish. An excellent performance of technically challenging music.New Music for Two Voices is a dazzling exploration of vocal virtuosity that sets – and meets – a very high standard. Hopefully this premiere album by Susan Narucki and Kirsten Ashley Wiest will be the first of more to follow. New Music for Two Voices is available in digital download or CD format from: Bandcamp:HB Direct: The post Susan Narucki & Kirsten Ashley Wiest – New Music for Two Voices appeared first on Sequenza21.

items.album: Steve Reich at 90: ‘Music for 18 Musicians’ (The Clore Ballroom, Southbank Centre, London, 27 September 2026)
items.excerpt: Just when Steve Reich’s ninetieth birthday celebrations appeared to be drifting towards an inauspicious conclusion, along comes Charles Hazlewood and the Paraorchestra to gatecrash the party, tear up the rulebook, let loose a posse of Dionysian dancers on the scene, and transform a routine Reich event into a Bacchanalian rave. items.body: Just when Steve Reich’s ninetieth birthday celebrations appeared to be drifting towards an inauspicious conclusion, along comes Charles Hazlewood and the Paraorchestra to gatecrash the party, tear up the rulebook, let loose a posse of Dionysian dancers on the scene, and transform a routine Reich event into a Bacchanalian rave. This new take on Music for 18 Musicians provided a breath of fresh air amongst a raft of retrospective events—Reich remodelled and refracted through the prism of psychedelia and 1990s warehouse EDM, with perhaps a whiff of hippy idealism and transcendental meditation thrown in. I’m not sure whether the composer would have approved. Most of those present gleefully lapped it all up. Hazlewood is known for thinking creatively outside the box, but here he appeared to be operating according to a completely different set of Euclidean principles. To be sure, Reich’s music has been placed in a variety of unorthodox settings and spaces over the years, ranging from disused train station buildings and repurposed multistorey car parks to all manner of outdoor locations, so there was nothing inherently radical in presenting this classic work at Southbank Centre’s Clore Ballroom. Nevertheless, dotting the ensemble around the space went against Reich’s own recommended set-up, as did Hazlewood’s encouragement for everyone to move about the space as if viewing an audible sculpture in an art gallery. Likewise, the idea of dancers moving in and around the ensemble was not in itself revolutionary. Reich’s music, including Music for 18, has provided accompaniment to several dance productions in the past, notably those of Laura Dean Dancers and Musicians, and Anne Teresa De Keersmaeker’s Rosas dance company. However, the idea of interpolating freestyle, improvised movement seemed to fly in the face of the piece’s austerely conceptual pretext. Hazlewood rightly drew attention, in a brief announcement at the beginning of the evening, to a whole range of paradoxes that lie at the heart of Reich’s music—not least that between rigor and freedom—and it was certainly refreshing to see Music for 18 unfettered from its structuralist straitjacket. There’s certainly nothing wrong with shaking things up, so long as the intention is motivated by creative and artistic concerns rather than dramatic effect. While there’s no doubting that Hazlewood’s intentions were genuine, the results were not always persuasive. The dance element, pre-planned beforehand, tended to shift attention from the sonic experience to a visual one, and while the idea of encouraging the audience to move in and around the space was in keeping with Music for 18’s ‘immersive’ impact, this too became something of a distraction. Many members of the audience appeared to circumambulate the space in a kind of somnambulistic daze, and the whole point of the exercise—to listen more attentively to the music—seemed to go by the wayside. I can’t imagine for a moment that walking around while trying to avoid bumping into other people doing the same thing might in any way sharpen one’s focus on the complex layers and textures that underpin Reich’s groundbreaking work. Thankfully, most seemed to have had enough of moving around after the opening set of eleven pulsing chords. So much for walking as a gradual process. I remained firmly anchored to the vibraphone station—the composition’s ‘signal box’ and timekeeper—where the rest of the ensemble could be heard in more-or-less perfect balance. What seemed to get lost in all the theatrical paraphernalia was the music itself, which was a shame since the Paraorchestra’s performance was never less than impressive, and at times quite brilliant. Highlights included brightly hued, bell-like clarinet and vocal buildups in Sections II, IV and IX; surging tonic-dominant movement in the pianos in Section IIIa; warmly glowing and flowing marimba and vocal colours halfway through Section V; and excellent ensemble coordination in Section X. And despite my cautious reservations about the happening-style multimedia nature of the performance, Sections VI–VIII, with their infectious maracas groove, yielded an extraordinarily uplifting synergy between music, dance and movement. At that moment, the entire performance clicked into place. As an experiment, this presentation of Music for 18 certainly possesses potential, but perhaps it’s worth taking a closer look at those early, gritty, grungy performances of minimalist music in New York’s large lofts and gallery spaces during the late 1960s and early ’70s. Photos of these early performances show audiences scattered about the venue, as was the case here, but sitting (or lying down) on cushions rather than walking around, with an amplified ensemble positioned at the centre of the room. Perhaps future audiences should be encouraged instead to bring a beanbag, lie back, and let the music wash over them, wave after beautiful wave… The post Steve Reich at 90: ‘Music for 18 Musicians’ (The Clore Ballroom, Southbank Centre, London, 27 September 2026) appeared first on Sequenza21.

items.body: In a house in Lomé, a woman kept a set of ceremonial pots she used for preparing potions for the older women of the Vodun temples. Vodun is the West African religion the Ewe and Fon have practised across Togo and Benin for centuries, the one that crossed the Atlantic on slave ships and became Haitian Vodou and Louisiana Voodoo. Its spirits are bound up with natural forces and they are reached through drumming and singing, so those women sang constantly. Her grandson grew up believing all that singing had gone into the clay and stayed there. Years later he took the pots and built a drum kit out of them. His name is Toto Tchilatchi, and half of what Nana Benz du Togo carry onto a stage is those pots. The other half is a bass David Kasanku built out of PVC drainpipe. He used to play bass, then spent four years assembling the gazé tuyau. Once it went underneath Toto’s kit, the pots and drums came to life, and together they made a groove full of sub-bass and complex polyrhythms. That groove became the bedrock for three singers, Lady Apoc, Parus Kekeli and Izealedu, with a small vintage Korg keyboard alongside their voices. The band’s word for what all of it adds up to is trance. They describe Vodun itself as being about rhythm, trance, nature and connection, and Lady Apoc says theirs comes from “repetitive energy.“ None of the five knew each other until 2019, when Peter Solo, the leader of Vaudou Game, came to Lomé to run a workshop and brought local musicians and artists together for it. Out of that workshop came the band, and Solo has produced them ever since. They took their name from the Nana Benz, the wax-print traders of Lomé’s central market who drove Mercedes-Benz cars and were confided in by the powerful. The band say they admire the courage and force those women showed in patriarchal societies. They sing in English, French and Mina, over the Vodun scales of the snake, Dan, and of Mami Wata, about women and the earth, and they say protecting one is inseparable from protecting the other. Their feminism, the band say, comes from the strength and resilience of African women, and their ecology from Vodun itself, and they say protecting women and protecting the earth cannot be pulled apart. Like many people of their generation, they grew up with mixed feelings about Vodun and were taught to be ashamed of parts of it, and at some point they moved away from it. Going back gave them their voice back. They stopped trying to fit into a musical category and started creating from who they are. Even so, they never set out to put Vodun in the spotlight, and years of work in the shadows came before they dared to get on a stage. Their first concert in Europe was Transmusicales de Rennes in 2022, and AGO followed the year after, recorded at the OTODI studio in Lomé with Solo producing. They went back to OTODI in December 2024 to record SÉ NAM, again with Solo, and it came out in June 2025. Its eleven tracks have a more contemporary production and more room for groove and rhythm. The title means “understand me” in Mina, one of the three languages they sing in. In October they bring it to WOMEX in Las Palmas… For this episode of Musical Road to WOMEX they answered our questions about how Vodun meets the dancefloor, what their handmade instruments do and what they hope to find on the island: they want to hear the timple, meet local musicians and find out what traces of African and Atlantic exchange can still be heard in Canarian music, and they arrive, as they put it, with their ears open. The playlist at the end lets you hear what they are bringing. You’ve been described as pioneers of “digital voodoo”. For someone hearing you for the first time, how would you introduce the meeting of Vodun tradition and the dancefloor? For us, Digital Vodou is not about taking something old and trying to make it modern. It is about showing that Vodun is already alive and has always had the power to evolve. Vodun is about rhythm, trance, nature and connection. And the dancefloor can be a place for that too. People come together, move together, let go. We bring traditional rhythms, songs, percussion and the handmade instruments we create into electronic music, bass and contemporary sounds. For us, it is a meeting between something very old and something that is still being born. That is what makes it feel both ancestral and futuristic. The band takes its name from the Nana Benz, the market women who turned the wax-print trade into power and independence. What did diving back into your Vodun heritage, after leaving it behind, open up for you musically? It gave us our voice back. Like many people from our generation, we grew up with mixed feelings about Vodun. There were things we were taught to be ashamed of, so at some point we moved away from it. Coming back to it changed the way we saw ourselves. We realised that Vodun is not only a spiritual tradition. It is also a way of understanding our relationship with the earth, with women, with our ancestors and with each other. And musically, it opened a whole world for us: rhythms, melodies, stories, symbols. Things that were already inside us. We stopped trying to fit into a musical category. We started creating from who we really are. WOMEX lands this year in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, an Atlantic island whose own traditions ride on the timple, a five-string guitar that carries both African and Latin American trade routes. What are you most curious to discover there? We are curious about the connections between the different traditions. Islands are special places. Cultures arrive there, meet, change and survive. We want to hear the timple, meet local musicians and discover what traces of African and Atlantic exchanges can still be heard in Canarian music. And honestly, we are excited about the unexpected. Maybe one of our handmade instruments will meet a sound from the island in a way we never imagined. That is what we love about music. Your instruments are handmade and upcycled, the gazé tuyaux among them, and your themes are feminist and ecological. In a WOMEX programme full of traditions, what makes your sound and your message unmistakably yours? For us, everything is connected. The recycled instruments are not just something you see on stage. They are part of our sound and part of the way we think. We take things that people throw away and give them another life. In a way, we do the same with our stories and traditions. We take things that have been misunderstood or pushed aside and bring them back into the present. Our feminism comes from the strength and resilience of African women. And our connection to ecology comes from Vodun itself. We often say, “Whoever does not respect women does not respect nature.” For us, that says a lot about who Nana Benz Du Togo is. WOMEX is built on unexpected meetings. Which artists, labels or collaborators are you hoping to cross paths with in Las Palmas? We don’t really have a list of names. We want to meet people who are deeply connected to where they come from but are not afraid to experiment. Artists who can move between tradition, ritual, electronic music, performance and new ideas. And that is one of the things we love about WOMEX. You can have a conversation with someone backstage and suddenly discover that there is something you can create together. We are coming with our ears open. You’ve toured Europe and built a reputation as a live force. Does a room of delegates and music professionals change how you bring the trance and the groove of your set? Not really. Of course, we know that WOMEX is important and that there will be a lot of professionals in the room. But once we are on stage, we have to be ourselves. Whether there are one hundred people, a thousand people or music professionals watching us, we want the same thing: for people to feel the music in their bodies. We want them to forget for a moment who they are supposed to be and simply become part of the rhythm. That is when the magic happens. “Voodoo is Nature,” you’ve said. Gran Canaria is a volcanic island shaped by the ocean around it. Does a landscape like that speak to the ecology at the heart of your songs? Absolutely. When you see a volcanic landscape, you are reminded that the earth is alive. It is powerful, it changes, it moves. For us, nature is not something outside of us. In Vodun, it is a living presence. The ocean, the wind, the stone, the fire inside the earth, these are not just things around us. They are forces. So being on an island shaped by the ocean and volcanoes feels very familiar to our way of thinking. It reminds us that we are part of something much bigger than ourselves. Your work carries a clear message about women’s strength and respect for the planet. Is there something you feel especially compelled to say through this showcase? Yes. We want to remind people that protecting women and protecting the earth are not separate things. We believe our traditions can still teach us something about that balance. We are not trying to go back to the past. We are trying to understand what we can take from it to imagine a different future. For us, women are creators, transmitters, protectors and forces of transformation. That is something we want to celebrate through our music. After SÉ NAM, what’s next? New recordings, new collaborations, directions you’re keen to push the project toward? SÉ NAM was an important chapter for us, but we already feel the next one coming. We are working on new music and pushing the dialogue between ritual percussion, the instruments we make ourselves and electronic production even further. We also want to work with artists from other parts of Africa, the Caribbean and Latin America. There are so many shared histories, rhythms and spiritual connections across the Atlantic that we would love to explore. We want to keep moving forward without losing our roots. If you could write a personal invitation to the people of Las Palmas to come and discover your showcase, what would it say? Come with your body before your expectations. Come to dance, listen, feel and maybe remember something older than all of us. We are bringing rhythms from Togo, women’s voices, handmade instruments and the energy of Digital Vodou. Don’t just come and watch us. Come and experience it with us. If you join us, we will create the ceremony together.   On 23 October at the Plaza Stage in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, Nana Benz du Togo will ask the WOMEX crowd to forget for a moment who they are supposed to be and become part of the rhythm   PLAYLIST: NANA BENZ DU TOGO X RHYTHM PASSPORT   You can find all the previous episodes of Musical Road to Womex HERE   The post Musical Road to WOMEX 2026 – Nana Benz du Togo appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Psalm 68 says Ethiopia will stretch out her hands to Elohim, one of the Hebrew Bible’s names for God, and Rastafari read the verse as prophecy, fulfilled when Haile Selassie I took the Ethiopian throne in 1930. Julian Asher, a reggae singer from Cape Town now living in Berlin, paraphrased it in the notes to his debut EP, Haile Abeba Sound, and on “Elohim” he builds a whole song around the name. He sings of a He and a She arriving at full strength to reclaim an ancient throne from those who lead people astray, and calls on Abba and Selassie I by name across the verses. The music comes from Downtown Steppas, a Berlin backing band who also build their own riddims. The partnership goes back to “Perilous” in 2022, and “Just Cause”, a single Asher cut over the band’s Fantasia riddim, now shares its name with their first album together. Just Cause was recorded last winter, from songs singer and band had been playing together for years. Stream “Elohim” HERE The post Daily Discovery: Julian Asher & Downtown Steppas – Elohim appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Review by JuanSaavedra — I was lucky enough to receive a promo copy of this album ahead of its October 2nd release through ARQUEN Records (many thanks, the guys from Spain are always so generous and I am very grateful), and I had already fallen for the three singles before hearing the full thing. So by the time I sat down with Datura Lodge in its entirety, I came in with high expectations. And somehow they were exceeded.2026 has been, honestly, a somewhat quiet year for new progressive rock releases that have genuinely grabbed me, while I wait for the new Steven Wilson album, which I am very much looking forward to. Which makes it all the more satisfying when something like this arrives. And curiously, reading the credits of this album, I discover that drummer Russell Holzman is also the drummer on the upcoming Steven Wilson record, and that his father Adam Holzman, whose career includes Miles Davis and Steven Wilson himself, plays keyboards here. A detail that says a lot about the calibre of this project.Nicky B and "W", the New Jersey duo at the heart of this project, have put together a debut that feels both deeply rooted in the tradition and completely alive in the present. The reference points are there if you want to find them. There is something of Genesis in the quieter, more introspective passages, and when the vocalist climbs to his upper register, the resemblance to Phil Collins is striking in the best possible way. There are moments that bring Porcupine Tree and Steven Wilson to mind, particularly in the layered textures and the way the album handles emotional weight. And Pink Floyd surfaces here and there, mostly in the atmosphere rather than anything overt. But none of this sounds like pastiche. It sounds like a band that has absorbed all of this and made something genuinely their own.The album opens with a trio of tracks, "Mummy", "Stone" and "98 and 94", that flow into each other almost like a suite and hook you before you even realise it. The middle section gets more direct and rock-driven, with "Can" and "Them" showing another side of the duo, harder-hitting and with that energy that recalls Rush. And "Hole", the third single, has that unmistakable Floydian atmosphere, a slow emotional build that keeps growing until the guitar solo says everything the words could not.But it is "Lodge", the closing track, that for me ties everything together. It starts with an acoustic delicacy that evokes the best moments of Genesis, and from there it grows into something wider and more modern without ever losing the melodic thread. It is the most complete track on the album and a finale that stays with you for days. Ben Karas also leaves an electrifying violin on "Stone" that is one of the most memorable moments of the whole listen.The album flows perfectly, has an ideal running time and not a single moment of filler. One of the most addictive listens I have had all year, and one I keep returning to without any sense of it diminishing. I can't wait to see where this band goes next. What a debut. Awesome album.

items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — To Keep the flame alive, to know how to rekindle it when needed. To show perseverance and courage to face difficulties, tragedies, absences, and times that aren't always favorable?standing tall, against all odds, despite the captain's age. These are the qualities Vittorio Nocenzi had to bring together to resurrect Banco Del Mutuo Soccorso in the 2010s, to pull it back from the darkness where so many of our illusions were lost, and to bring to fruition the surprising *Transiberiana* in 2019, followed by *Orlando, la forma dell'amore*, the second album by the band's new lineup, that is to say, without Gianni, who has been pursuing a solo career since the '80s, and without Giacomo or Rodolfo, who departed without a trace for the highest heavens, the realm of the musical geniuses of our time. It's hard not to draw a parallel with PFM, another legendary figure of the Italian progressive rock scene during the "imperial decade." For both bands, we've witnessed a splendid comeback after a period?long or short?of inactivity, creative stagnation, or even alarming setbacks (the mid-1980s), a return to the forefront of the prog scene led by a founding member (Franz Di Cioccio for PFM), a shared desire to return to more ambitious compositions mixed with more straightforward ones, and a shared ability to surround themselves with new, highly talented musician friends and lyricists, as well as a young recruit who brings a certain sense of the spirit of the times (Vittorio's son from Banco and Luca Zabbini of Barock Project, who contributed keyboards and composition to more than half of PFM's latest album). The result is a similar musical style: smooth symphonic prog blended with vigorous jazz-rock. Without wanting to pit them against each other, I tended to give a slight edge to PFM's latest album (I Dreamed of Electric Sheep) as Zabbini's talent as a composer sometimes makes all the difference. But Banco's unbridled romanticism, magnified by an exceptional new singer (the impressive Tony D'Alessio), may give it greater and more lasting appeal. With the help of his son Michaelangelo and lyricist Paolo Lugli, Vittorio Nocenzi presents *Orlando*, an ambitious and highly compelling concept album, both for its subject matter (inspired by the famous chivalric poem *Orlando Furioso*, composed in the early 16th century by Ludovico Ariosto?known as "l'Arioste"?as a sequel to Matteo Maria Boiardo's *Orlando Innamorato*) and for its generous running time (nearly 80 minutes, the equivalent of a double album from the vinyl era) and the form it takes (progressive instrumentals straight out of the '70s, an 11-minute epic, a refreshing diversity?), as well as by its determination to return to the roots of RPI right from the start of the record (the formidable "Proemio"/"La Pianura Rossa" sequence). With melodies that hit the mark, a rich use of keyboards featuring dizzying Moog solos, nods to the past, sparkling rhythms, and harmonic inventiveness that rarely falters, *Orlando* seems to follow in the musical footsteps of its predecessor, while going a step further on the path back to its roots, bringing us all those poignant memories that are more like scents than thoughts. As you listen more and more, you quickly forget the few moments that are a bit saccharine ("L'Amore Accade"), dull ones ("Serve Orlando Adesso"), incongruous ones (the bandoneon tango in "Non Mi Spaventa Pi� L'amore"), or even questionable ones (the overly conventional blues of "Non Credere Alla Luna")?and instead focus on the remaining 60 minutes, a level of quality rarely achieved by Banco since the late '70s, with a few major highlights such as "Le Anime Deserte Del Mondo" (The Deserted Souls of the World?what a beautiful title!), where the best of Banco's golden age comes together for five divine minutes with Kate Bush (on bass), Keith Emerson (on repetitive piano), PFM, and Battiato. A delicate harmony emerges from this unlikely blend, as if the graceful notes in this track were passing through a mysterious filter. "L'isola Felice" is another irresistible moment, bewildering with its Caribbean-style intro, xylophone, and subtle electronic backdrop, its monotone yet edgy vocals, and its unexpected Hammond organ solo. But for the listener, this track is indeed all about bliss and rapture. Some may prefer "Cadere O Volare," which the band premiered in a video a few months ago and which is described as "the perfect musical synthesis of this album, a perfect example of the variety of arrangements," ranging from a classical string quartet intro to the electric guitar of the best jerky Italian pop of the '80s, and culminating in a '60s-style Hammond organ solo after passing through a quiet, acoustic interlude. Yet another resounding success. Added to the two instrumentals?which are hard to resist?we have here five little gems of modern Italian pop that shine so brightly they manage to outshine the lengthy "Moon Suite" (11:49), which is by no means without merit. Memorable above all for its first section?in the purest, dynamic Banco style?and for the melodic finesse of its second section, this highly anticipated long progressive suite generally lives up to its promise. Despite a few weaknesses and its length, *Orlando, le forme dell'amore* comes closest to what one would expect from a fascinating Banco?a band capable of blending the sound and spirit of contemporary melodic rock with a more traditional transalpine prog without being stuck in the past, and capable of transporting you to another dimension. After more than 50 years, Banco remains a living legend, bringing the tale of Sir Roland to life in modern terms and through music embroidered with jazz-prog gold via a rich and generous new album?even if it isn't consistently thrilling or ideally progressive (and vice versa).

items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — *I Dreamed of Electric Sheep* (titled *Ho Sognato Pecore Elettriche* in its Italian version) naturally refers to the book written by P.K. Dick in 1966 (*Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?*?the question remains open) and, more specifically, to the 1982 film *Blade Runner* directed by Ridley Scott. Drawing inspiration from these two masterpieces, PFM has created a concept album that, much like the main character in Dick's work, constantly asks what sets us apart from androids and what defines our humanity?or rather, what remains of our humanity when we spend our days and nights isolated and alone, lost in front of a computer or smartphone screen. Such a powerful subject deserved music of equal strength. But would PFM?that pioneering trailblazer, capable of producing four cornerstones of the RPI in a row from 1972 to 1975?be able to recapture the musical inspiration of its greatest moments? The chaotic career this famous Italian band has experienced since the late 1970s remains etched in our memories. That dizzying decline after 1977?followed by a slight improvement in quality with the album *Mrs. Baker* ten years later, a more or less convincing comeback in 1997, and the handful of interesting albums that followed, though lacking the genius of their early days?would have been enough to leave us skeptical. But four years ago, the well-crafted *Emotional Tattoos*, consisting of new compositions, which hadn't happened in 10 years, had restored our confidence and hope in the talent of the Milanese musicians, though it did little to console us for the absence of Flavio Premoli and Franco Mussida, two of the three pillars who, along with drummer Franz Di Cioccio, formed the soul of the band. Today, only Di Cioccio remains from the original lineup?the sole member to have appeared on every PFM album. And while he is no longer the wildly inventive drummer of *Photos of Ghosts* or *Chocolate Kings*, his performance throughout this new album is quite respectable, especially considering his advanced age (75 years old in 2021). All the more so because, for the first time in a long while, he is the sole drummer here, without handing the reins to someone younger than him, in addition to handling the vocals. At his side are two veterans: the loyal Swiss bassist Patrick Djivas, as well as violinist Lucio Fabbri, who has been part of PFM since 1979. On guitar is the virtuoso Marco Sfogli, whom we've seen perform alongside James Labrie and who was already featured on the previous album. Alessandro Scaglione, the band's official keyboardist for the past decade, rounds out the core lineup. He occasionally steps aside for Luca Zabbini, the brilliant leader of Barock Project (which gives us the opportunity to mention him twice in this issue). We also find?and this is no small surprise?Flavio Premoli contributing some delightful passages on the Mini Moog. With such a talented group of musicians and composers, we could expect nothing less than the best. And "Mondi parallel / Worlds Beyond" (3:19) doesn't disappoint right from the start of the album. It says it all in three minutes. We immediately find ourselves thinking that this is a beautiful window onto what could be PFM's full-fledged return to the energetic and imaginative symphonic progressive rock that made them unique and magnificent in the '70s?hoping that this isn't just a glimpse behind the curtain of that fabulous past. Refreshing. "Umani alieni / Adrenaline Oasis" (4:53) starts off slowly, at least at first, then quickly transforms into a fluid and frenzied RPI, a blend of neo-prog and transalpine folk ambiance. With a touch of high-octane Branduardi. Mind-blowing. "Ombre amiche / "Let Go" (4:06) is a beautiful song with a '90s vibe, perfectly crafted, elaborate, and performed with more emotion than imagination. In its structure, melody, certain synth sounds, and even in the performance, we seem to recognize a subtle tribute to the late Franco Battiato, who cruelly left us last spring. Moving. "La grande corsa / City Life" (5:01) takes a more ambitious approach to modern neo-prog (is Frost* trying his hand at RPI?), firmly rooted in 21st-century prog to deliver one of the album's highlights, even though it's relatively far removed from the splendor and style of the past. Powerful. "AtmoSpace / If I Had Wings" (4:23) is a more pronounced nod to their idol Battiato, whether through the master's characteristic melody, the philosophical-poetic lyrics, the distinctive sound, or?above all?the work on the vocals and singing. Kudos to PFM for attempting, with this original track?unique in their discography?to revive and place on the pedestal he deserves this Sicilian genius who remains all too little known in our part of the world. Haunting. "Pecore elettriche / Electric Sheep" (4:09) is a prog rock track with a deceptively funky vibe?effective but a bit too formulaic to win our full and complete endorsement, despite Djivas's impressive bass playing and a Hammond organ part that underpins and legitimizes the whole piece with its solidity and virtuosity. This track could be seen as the album's minor weak spot?a relative weakness that's quickly forgiven. Enjoyable. "Mr. Non Lo So / Daily Heroes" (3:48), also slightly funky, nevertheless moves into a different hybrid register?a bit hard rock, a bit bluesy, elusive, and quite close to what Deep Purple might do these days. Lucio Fabbri and his violin take center stage, bringing the whole thing back to a more classical RPI sound. It's catchy. "Il respiro del tempo / Kindred Souls" (6:19) evokes a Celtic atmosphere, much like "Quartier Generale" did on the previous album, with an added touch of melancholy?a bit like Simple Minds used to do in the '80s. It's also an opportunity to welcome distinguished guests: Steve Hackett and Ian Anderson, in person and remotely! Added to this are some highly inspired contributions from Flavio Premoli?true nods to the band's most glorious past?leaving us utterly spellbound. Delightful. "Transumanza" (1:07) and "Transumanza Jam" (3:39) bring the album to a rousing close with Zabbini's Moog and Hammond organ solos, sure to make us roar with delight. All of PFM's musicians let loose on this wild track, young and old alike. A must-have, especially for those who, like me, loved the virtuosic flights of fancy and progressive excesses of Santana during the *Welcome* or *Borboletta* era. Much shorter than its predecessor, the highly regarded "Emotional Tattoos" released in 2017 (40' vs. 60'), "I Dreamed of Electric Sheep" consistently sounds like top-notch PFM and thus avoids the occasional sentimentality or mid-tempo clich�s that had still been present to some extent up until then. PFM, the most legendary of the RPI bands, is a living legend with an exceptional longevity that commands respect (over 50 years), passionately led by a Franz Di Cioccio who seems rejuvenated. Tired of constantly treading on the remnants of a lost progressive inspiration, PFM returns today as fresh as on day one to enthusiastically?if not head-on?embrace the RPI of its youth, along with the place it rightfully deserves: that of one of the first and greatest Italian progressive bands of all time. Irresistible.

items.body: Review by arcane-beautiful — Solaris by The Ocean is a great step forward for the German sludgy atmospheric prog metallers, allowing new vocalists Enrico Tiberi & Lane Shi great room to show off their unique talents. Musically more epic since their Phanerozoic album series, it sees the band create longer compositions that gives great drama and atmosphere. While I was a massive fan of former vocalist L�ic Rossetti, Tiberi's cleans and barks are a perfect replacement, adding the same drama and emotion but with his own unique flair, while Shi's unique chants and screams are an extra dimension to the bands sound, which adds an almost creepy mood to the thick atmosphere the band create. The use of industrial electronic noises throughout are also great at adding mood to the overall pieces. I'd give this a mid 8 out of 10. The track I'd recommend is Belligerence.

(4th in arow if you ask me!)They are back to a heavier sound, after the softer and more reflective Coming Up to Consciousness.Still, there are a lot of new experimentations, and it is their proggiest album in the discography,especially due to the 2 larger tracks. The production/mixing was done by Bruce Soord which is shownin a beautiful and balanced composition: the guitars sound heavy but also very crispy with tightsounding and the drums are beautiful and probably the best mix in their discography.All the trademark elements of PRR are here: Heavy and groovy guitars, very grunge and industrialsounding, distorted soundscapes, eletronic passages and multi-layared vocals.Standout tracks are Black-Arrow Acrobats and Hold Your Wrath, featuring unexpected turns, ambience,creative chord progressions and build ups. Spin Like Fire and Haywire Heart are explosive rockingstandout singles. Rumination Ruin is an excellent companion to the sublime title track and BelowRadiance is a more electronic piece with a beautiful composition and ambience.

items.body: Review by sgtpepper — The first APP album has captured hearts of many progressive and pop enthusiasts.It sounded contemporary, even futuristic (vocal vocoder) with the clean, imaginative production and the great concept selection with the another Al(l)an, Edgar Alan Poe.In comparison to the later albums, music is not that radio friendly yet and music keeps being ambitious and focused, where the duel among vocalists vs instrumentals are pretty levelled.The band shows knack for emotional ballads ("The Cask of Amontillado", "To one in paradise") which will be perfected on other albums. I have always liked the symbiose of emotional music, great studio talent (no surprise when speaking of Alan Parsons) and curious instrumentals. The flagship of all APP instrumentals is presented on the second side of the album "The fall of the house of Usher". It comprises 5 parts, all of them both progressive and symphonic without any playing excesses.No wonder this album belongs to the highest acclaimed APP albums and carved a unique blend of styles on the European music map.

items.body: This is the first of a projected three-CD series that will include Emilie Mayer’s complete surviving orchestral works played on period instruments. Several recordings of Mayer’s orchestral oeuvre have been issued over the last decade, including four CDs on CPO that include all surviving orchestral music as well as a reconstruction of the fourth symphony. Mayer’s time has finally arrived, and this new recording is further proof, if any is still needed, that this music is fully worth our attention. Emilie Mayer, Vol. 1 Amazon Presto Apple This program (with almost 80 minutes of music) includes the overtures in D minor and C major (No. 3), Mayer’s one and only concerto for piano in B-flat major, and her first symphony. These Akademie für Alte Musik Berlin performances are consistently energetic and quick-paced: this is the fastest of three recordings of the concerto, and the symphony is about a minute faster than CPO’s recording with the NDR Radiophilharmonie under Leo McFall. While some period instrument ensembles adopt a weightier, more homogeneous string sound for late Classical and Romantic music, the AAM Berlin continues to play with lean, silvery strings (7/7/4/4/3) that resolutely avoid vibrato. With its fruity and characterful woodwinds, the sound world offered here is substantially different from earlier recordings. I was most impressed by the performance of the concerto. We do not know when Mayer composed it (she did not date her manuscripts), but it is her most overtly classical work, Mozartian in substance and style. Its fast outer movements feature a great deal of virtuosic filigree, which Alexander Melnikov dispatches with deceptive ease. Interplay between the piano and orchestra has an intimacy and joie de vivre that outshines the overly earnest performance by Ewa Kupiec (Neubrandenburger Philharmonie/Stefan Malzew/Capriccio). AAM Berlin also find more rhythmic lift than do the Kölner Akademie and Michael Alexander Willens (CPO) accompanying pianist Tobias Koch. Melnikov draws out a greater variety of colors from his 1867 Blüthner. Yet I find Kupiec best in the slow second movement, where she finds a richer strain of lyricism than either of her colleagues. Both overtures are expertly played here, though Willens’ CPO renditions of both (found on the same recording as the piano concerto) are a tad quicker and more dramatically telling. Emilie Mayer (©️ The Classic Review, AI generated) The first symphony reveals a vivid compositional imagination. The opening movement’s brooding slow introduction is a funeral march in all but name, followed by an urgent Allegro energico. The energy of this new reading is undeniable, but the ensemble, closely recorded in a dry hall, lacks sufficient weight to fully capture the music’s dramatic twists and turns. The NDR Radiophilharmonie, led by Leo McFall, is similarly energetic, with winds balanced well to the fore, but has an added weightiness that better serves Mayer’s dramatic writing. The same is true of the third movement, which features contrasts of color, range and dynamics. The AAM Berlin cellos and basses play with gusto, but their small numbers cannot match the heft of the NDR performance. The NDR reading is particularly impressive in the Adagio, where the woodwind arabesques positively cry out for greater flexibility and rubato than the AAM Berlin’s concertmaster Bernhard Forck allows. McFall is only about 30 seconds slower, but he allows for more give and take in the phrasing, which draws out a more melancholic strain from the writing. An instance, perhaps, where a conductor’s leadership and shaping make for a more emotionally convincing reading. Harmonia Mundi’s ancillary materials are excellent, with especially informative notes by Linus Bickmann. These AAM Berlin performances are first-rate, but for me the sonority and leadership from the podium make the NDR symphony performance more involving, though I believe no one has quite realized the work’s full dramatic potential. Still, there is much to admire here, and I look forward to hearing future releases in this series. Recommended Comparisons Emilie Mayer: Symphony No. 1 NDR Radiophilharmonie, Leo McFall Emilie Mayer: Piano Concerto in B-flat major Ewa Kupiec The form can be filled in the actual website url. items.body: Hey friends, quick update from the Senior Staff on the eve of the spooky season. It’s been real busy for us in both in non-IDUD related life stuff, and as such it’s very possible we are overlooking new records and artists that we should have our eye on. Thus it’s time for a renewal of our annual plea to please, tell us what we haven’t covered that you think would be to our taste. You can do it right here in the comments of this very post? As much as we enjoy a good dig through Bandcamp and various setlists from respected DJs and friends, we’d love a blindspot check from our readers, who have generally never steered us wrong with that sort of thing. We’d sure appreciate it. Seven Trees Mesh, “Trying to Save You” Bristol’s Mesh are such a unique quantity in the big umbrella that is Our Thing. Taking synthpop and rendering them with rock band energy isn’t the easiest move in music, but they’ve always pulled it off with aplomb. See new single “Trying to Save You” from the forthcoming mini-album “Fallen Angel” for example; big hooks, bold arrangement choices (that switch up as it exits the chorus is so clever) and lots of momentum. Truly no other band sounds like them. Fallen Angel by Mesh Aurat, “XIII” Coming just a few months after the dense and spiky Cobra EP, this teaser from Aurat’s forthcoming silhouette LP portends something quite different from the highly touted and fast moving LA act. Forsaking their EBM tendencies, this cut carries their goth/post-punk genome into unexpected doomgaze territory. Is it reflective of the whole release? We’ll be sure to follow up in a month’s time. silhouette by Aurat Kontravoid, “Chances” Kontravoid is no stranger to writing a great electro-pop jam; you could probably build a decent mixtape out of cuts from across the catalogue like “Too Deep”, “Losing Game” and “Faceless”. Strong possibility you’d throw “Chances”, another taste of the upcoming Sound of the Void to that list also, it’s exactly the kind of catchy, danceable, melancholic but forceful cut that Cam Findlay has been casually knocking out for some time now. We wouldn’t be shocked to hear this at any given goth club or darkwave party over the next couple of years, it’s fun and spooky in the right ways. Sound of the Void by Kontravoid Chalice Sect, “Silent Fever” Chalice Sect is a new name to us but it doesn’t take long to cotton onto the LA act’s rhythmically pummelling read on darkwave on this track from their forthcoming Finis Initii EP. A slew of heavily distorted synths which sound as though they have more in common with the aggro side of synthwave than goth drives things further into a maximalist space which will likely irritate purists but probably goes off live quite well. Finis Initii by Chalice Sect Nasdrowie, “Impact” Shout-out to friend Nick for bringing this EP from Nadrowie to our attention. It’s largely instrumental, but the vocals on “Impact” position it as the sort of murky 90s electro industrial that is like candy to us. Raw and rough, you could hear this being spun in a set with any number of classic Zoth bands. For fans of Evil’s Toy, and maybe Seven Trees? A New World To Cry by Nasdrowie Seven Trees, “Underneath My Skin” Speak of the devil, here’s a pleasantly moody and stark new cut from the aforementioned reactivated Swedish dark electro vets Seven Trees. As with their 2021 comeback LP Dead/End “Underneath My Skin” isn’t trying to leap off the page at you, but as the simple but solid structure beneath the clean and icy programming rolls along, the track progressively builds a sense of dread and inevitability that leaves a lasting chill. Solid and considered stuff for those who prioritize mood and affect in their dark electro. Underneath My Skin by Seven Trees The post Tracks: September 27th, 2026 appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items.body: LA-based supergroup Beauty In Chaos released their fifth studio album, “Quiet Place”, on 28 September 2026 through 33.3 Music Collective. The date is exactly eight years after their debut, “Finding Beauty in Chaos”, which came out on 28 September 2018 on the same label. Quiet Place by Beauty In Chaos The project is led by guitarist Michael Ciravolo, formerly of Human Drama and Gene Loves Jezebel and currently President of Schecter Guitars. “Quiet Place” was recorded, mixed and produced by Grammy-nominated producer Michael Rozon at SAINTinLA Studio, with Tim Perry of 33.3 Music Collective as executive producer, mastering by Dale Becker and cover paintings by Maren Platzhoff. Ten core tracks make up the album, each featuring a different vocalist. Returning contributors include Ashton Nyte of The Awakening on lead track “Home”, Cinthya Hussey (assisted by her husband, The Mission frontman Wayne Hussey), Whitney Tai, Julian Shah-Tayler, Betsy Martin, Leo Luganskiy and Kommunity FK’s Patrik Mata. Nick Schultz, formerly of The Faces Of Sarah, and Strangelove’s Brent Meyer join the Beauty In Chaos roster for the first time. The album’s focus track is “You Made Me A Weapon”, featuring Julian Shah-Tayler. The lead single, “Home”, reunites Ciravolo with Nyte, who also sang on the band’s first single, “Storm”, eight years earlier. Nyte directed and edited the “Home” video, filmed together with longtime collaborator Vicente Cordero of Industrialism Films, and featuring Nyte on vocals, Ciravolo on guitar and Tish Ciravolo on bass. Michael Ciravolo describes “Quiet Place” as “quite possibly our most diverse album, with a collection of songs that just work together.” He said the writing sessions with Rozon kept producing new material, but that he chose to stop at ten core tracks so the album could still land on the same date as the band’s debut. The Deluxe CD edition adds three cover-song tracks, on which Ciravolo himself sings: “God’s Gonna Cut You Down”, “Get Down Moses” and “Dancing Barefoot”. “Quiet Place” is also available as a 100-copy limited edition, a 180g double vinyl pressed on Ocean Blue Glitter, hand-numbered and packaged with an eight-page lyric booklet, a bonus CD and three Beauty In Chaos guitar picks; a “Goth Black” double vinyl and a digital version are sold through the band’s own store, alongside streaming on Bandcamp, Spotify and Apple Music. About Beauty In Chaos Beauty In Chaos is a Los Angeles-based collaborative project put together by guitarist Michael Ciravolo, formerly of Human Drama and Gene Loves Jezebel. He launched it in 2018 with the debut album “Finding Beauty in Chaos”, released on 28 September 2018 via 33.3 Music Collective and produced by Michael Rozon at SAINTinLA Studio. That first record brought together guests including Al Jourgensen of Ministry, Simon Gallup of The Cure, Ashton Nyte of The Awakening, Michael Aston of Gene Loves Jezebel, Robin Zander of Cheap Trick, Michael Anthony of Van Halen, Ice-T, dUg Pinnick of King’s X and Wayne Hussey of The Mission. A remix companion, “Beauty Re-Envisioned”, followed in 2019. Since then, Beauty In Chaos has released a stream of singles and full-lengths built around rotating vocalists, among them “The Kiss of the World” featuring Elena Alice Fossi of Kirlian Camera and Spectra*Paris, and the 2022 album “Behind the Veil”, built around an all-female cast of singers. In 2023, Beauty In Chaos and Julian Shah-Tayler released the single “Kiss Me (Goodbye)”. The fourth album, “Dancing With Angels”, followed in July 2024, preceded by the single “Holy Ground” and featuring a “Diving For Pearls” collaboration with Wayne Hussey and Cinthya Hussey of The Mission. A career-spanning compilation, “Hidden In Plain Sight, 2018-2025”, and the double A-side single “God’s Gonna Cut You Down” b/w “Get Down Moses” both arrived in late 2025. Across its now five studio albums, Beauty In Chaos has drawn on musicians connected to The Mission, The Cure, Ministry, Cheap Trick, The Offspring, Gene Loves Jezebel, Marilyn Manson, Human Drama, Bauhaus, Nine Inch Nails, Van Halen, A Flock of Seagulls and King’s X, among others. “Quiet Place” carries that same rotating-cast format into its eighth anniversary year.

items.body: Danish synthpop duo SoftWave will release “Through Open Eyes (Black Nail Cabaret Remix)” on 16 October 2026. It is the third and final single from “things we’ve remixed”, SoftWave’s remix album due on 23 October 2026, and it is remixed by Black Nail Cabaret, the Budapest duo of Emese “Emke” Árvai-Illés and Krisztián Árvai. The original “Through Open Eyes” is track seven on SoftWave’s second album, “things we’ve done”, released digitally on 13 October 2023. Black Nail Cabaret, built around Árvai-Illés’s vocals and Árvai’s keyboards, gives the song a darker, more atmospheric edge than the original. Two singles already lead into “things we’ve remixed”: “Supernova (Aspra Remix)”, reworked by Aspra, the solo project of Marsheaux member Sophia Sarigiannidou, and “Wake Up (Cicero Remix)”, remixed by Scottish synthpop artist Cicero and released on 18 September 2026. Catrine Christensen and Jerry Olsen have built a remix compilation into the release cycle of every SoftWave album since 2017. That pattern continues on “things we’ve remixed”, which draws contributors from several countries. About SoftWave SoftWave is the Danish duo of Catrine Christensen (vocals, lyrics) and Jerry Olsen (synthesizers, production), formed in 2014 and based at their own Blue Orange Studio. The pair name Erasure among their influences and describe their sound as a mix of classic British-styled synthpop and dance-pop. SoftWave’s debut EP, “Together Alone”, came out on 27 May 2016, followed by a remix collection, “Together Alone The Remixes”, in February 2017. The debut album, “Game On”, arrived in April 2019 on digital, CD and LP. Its own remix companion, “Game On 1Up”, came that November and was later reissued on CD by Electro-Shock Records. SoftWave supported OMD on the Scandinavian leg of the “Souvenir” tour in February 2020. The EP “Aspire” followed in October 2022, and the duo’s second album, “things we’ve done”, arrived in October 2023, later pressed to vinyl in June 2024. SoftWave has also remixed other artists’ work, including Cicero’s “Love Is Everywhere” for his “Future Boy” 30th-anniversary reissue in 2023. “Through Open Eyes (Black Nail Cabaret Remix)” now carries that same track from “things we’ve done” into the duo’s third remix album, out 23 October 2026.

items.body: Belgian gothic rock band Star Industry will release their 2007 album “Last Crusades” on vinyl for the first time on November 30, 2026, through Alfa Matrix. The LP is limited to 500 copies worldwide, priced at €18.99. ‘Last Crusades’ vinyl: format and tracklist The vinyl edition carries new artwork adapted for the LP format and reproduces the original ten-track album across two sides: A-side: “Lost Generation” “Pray” “Forever” “Out Of My Head” “Sin” B-side: “Last Crusades” “The Return Of David Gun” “Substitudes” “The Spirits Within” “Fall From Grace” “Last Crusades” was Star Industry’s third full-length album, originally released on April 20, 2007, and marked the band’s first release through Alfa Matrix. A digital version remains available on Bandcamp. Last crusades (Bonus Tracks Version) by STAR INDUSTRY Part of the Alfa Matrix Essentials vinyl series The “Last Crusades” LP is part of Alfa Matrix Essentials, a vinyl reissue series tied to the label’s 25th anniversary that brings catalogue albums to the format for the first time. Star Industry previously received the same treatment in 2020, when their 1997 debut album, “Iron Dust Crush,” was issued on vinyl for the first time. The band is currently working on a new studio album, scheduled for March 2027. About Star Industry Star Industry formed in 1996 in Maasmechelen, Belgium, when Arts Academy friends Peter Beckers, Stijn Kuijpers and Xavier Vranken united around a shared interest in early New Wave music. Marc Haerden (drums) and Peter Gerits (synths) joined shortly after, and the band recorded its debut material at Galaxy Studio. Star Industry played its first concert on April 12, 1998, at the Black Easter Festival in Ghent. The band’s debut album, “Iron Dust Crush,” was released independently in 1997 and later picked up by Purple Moon Records; its single “Nineties” topped Israel’s alternative chart the following year. A “New Millennium E.P.” followed in 1999 on the EuroRock Festival label, the same year drummer Kurt Lantin replaced Marc Haerden. The band’s second full-length album, “Velvet,” arrived in 2001. “Last Crusades,” released in 2007, marked Star Industry’s move to Alfa Matrix, followed by the live album “Black Angel White Devil,” recorded in Madrid in 2008. The band toured China in 2011, playing Hong Kong, Shanghai and Beijing, and made its United States debut at New York’s Tammany Hall in 2012. Synth player Rich Vanderhoven replaced Peter Gerits in 2015, the same year the band released the “Eilyne E.P.” and the album “The Renegade,” recorded at Motor Music Studio. Star Industry contributed a cover of “Stripped” to Alfa Matrix’s 2019 Depeche Mode tribute compilation. Co-founder and bassist Stijn Kuijpers died in 2021. Rich Vanderhoven moved from synths to bass, and Joël Vranken joined the band on synths. Star Industry’s current lineup is Peter Beckers (vocals, guitar), Xavier Vranken (lead guitar), Kurt Lantin (drums), Rich Vanderhoven (bass) and Joël Vranken (synths). The band has said its focus since Kuijpers’ death has been on completing a new studio album, due in March 2027.

The LP is limited to 300 copies worldwide, priced at €18.99, with no repress planned. ‘Harshlizer’ vinyl: format and tracklist The vinyl edition carries new artwork designed specifically for the LP format and reproduces the original ten-track album across two sides: A-side: “No Way Back” “Evil Bloody Music” “She’s On Drugs (more than me)” “See You In Hell (feat. Suicide Commando)” “Harshlizer” B-side: “Lies” “Control The Universe” “Nothing To Lose” “Far Away” “Her Blood Into My Veins” “Harshlizer” marked the start of Alien Vampires’ relationship with Alfa Matrix when it was first released in 2010, and includes “See You In Hell,” the duo’s collaboration with Suicide Commando. A digital version of the album, expanded with the “Industrializer” bonus disc of additional tracks and remixes released in 2024, remains available on Bandcamp. Harshlizer + Industrializer (Bonus Version) by Alien Vampires Part of the Alfa Matrix Essentials vinyl series The “Harshlizer” LP is part of Alfa Matrix Essentials, a vinyl reissue series tied to the label’s 25th anniversary that brings catalogue albums to the format for the first time. Alien Vampires previously released the limited-edition LP “Kinky To Hell” on solid red vinyl through Alfa Matrix in 2022. About Alien Vampires Alien Vampires is an Italian industrial, EBM and dark electro duo formed in 2003 by Nysrok Infernalien, who handles guitars and keyboards, alongside Nightstalker on keyboards and drums. The project released its debut single, “I’m Dead Fuck You,” in 2004, followed by the album “Evil Generation” in 2005 through Kold Finger. After the 2007 EP “Nuns Are Pregnant” and the album “No One Here Gets Out Alive” through BLC Productions, Alien Vampires released “Fuck Off and Die!” in 2009. “Harshlizer” arrived in 2010 as the duo’s first release through Alfa Matrix, a relationship that has continued since. Alfa Matrix issued a deluxe two-CD version of “Harshlizer” paired with the bonus disc “Industrializer” in February 2024, gathering additional tracks and remixes from the same period as the original album. Alien Vampires continued with the EPs “Clubbers Die Younger” (2012), “Hard Drugs & BDSM” (2014), “World in Denial” and “Destrudo” (both 2020), and the albums “Drag You to Hell” (2015), “Evil Degeneration Offspring” (2017) and “Fuck The Revolution Bring On The Apocalypse” (2018). “Drag You to Hell” featured collaborations with members of Ministry, Mayhem and Psyclon Nine. The duo’s most recent album, “Return Me To Hell,” followed in 2023 with a cover of Skinny Puppy’s “Assimilate” featuring former Slipknot drummer Joey Jordison, in one of his final recordings before his death.
